Shotcodes: CTD_AI_447_WindshieldCloud01; CTD_AI_447_WindshieldCloud02; CTD_AI_447_PitotTubes; CTD_AI_447_NoseUpward01; CTD_AI_447_NoseUpward02; CTD_AI_447_Nose12Degrees02; CTD_AI_447_PlaneClimbing; CTD_AI_447_PlanePlummets01
Problem: Eight briefs call for visible hail striking the windshield, pitot probes and airframe.
Correction: The BEA found the probes were obstructed by high-altitude ice crystals in a cumulonimbus anvil at FL350 — no hail; render fine ice crystals streaming past, not bouncing hailstones.

Problem: Exterior briefs show the A330 falling tail-first out of the sky.
Correction: The aircraft stayed nose-up at roughly 15–16° and mushed down flat/belly-first at about 10,900 ft/min for the whole 3.5-minute descent.

Problem: Brief has Captain Dubois grab the control from Bonin and push it forward.
Correction: Dubois re-entered at 02:11:43 and stood behind the two co-pilots for the rest of the flight; he never took the controls.

Problem: Cabin briefs specify the plane at a 45° angle with passengers pressed into their seats.
Correction: Pitch was about 15–16° nose-up at roughly 1g, so the floor should tilt only slightly, not steeply.

Problem: Establishing cockpit shot is slugged with the sun setting outside.
Correction: AF447 left Rio at 19:29 local, roughly two hours after sunset — the entire flight was in darkness.

Problem: The beat is about two pilots working engine thrust against each other, but the briefs stage it on the side-sticks.
Correction: Thrust is set on a single shared pair of levers on the centre pedestal — one pilot pulls to idle, the other pushes up six seconds later.

Problem: Brief calls for reactor building 2 to explode, camera engulfed in smoke.
Correction: Unit 2 never had a hydrogen explosion — its building stayed standing because the blowout panel had already opened; only units 1, 3 and 4 blew up.
Source: IAEA / World Nuclear Association Fukushima record

Problem: Three briefs show a tanker truck backing onto a dock and dumping tank water into the sea.
Correction: ALPS-treated water is diluted and released through a piped undersea tunnel about 1 km offshore; no tanker trucks are involved.

Problem: Briefs put workers with flashlights inside the reactor, around the core, reading a flashing MELTDOWN indicator.
Correction: The fuel is sealed inside the pressure vessel and physically unreachable; crews tracked surviving readings from the blacked-out control room, and no meltdown warning display exists.

Problem: Gauges are specified reading 5,000 Fahrenheit (one brief 500–1,200 with no unit).
Correction: Japanese plant instrumentation reads Celsius — fuel melting shows as roughly 2,800 °C, and the same scale must be used across the sequence.
Source: TEPCO plant documentation; UO₂ melting point ~2,800 °C

Problem: Briefs show firefighters hosing water onto reactor 1 until the hose runs dry, pegged to 7:30 PM.
Correction: Fire engines pumped through the plant's fire-protection line rather than spraying the building, and not until the early hours of 12 March.

Problem: Briefs stage a hall of about 250 suited workers being told to evacuate.
Correction: On 15 March roughly 650–750 workers withdrew to Daini leaving about 50–70 behind — check the 250 figure.

Problem: The approach to Lakehurst is briefed as a sunny day.
Correction: 6 May 1937 was overcast with thunderstorms and light rain at 7:25 PM — grey, rain-washed dusk. As briefed it also contradicts StormClouds and WeatherReport.

Problem: Brief asks for a 'hydrogen/helium pouch' rip, and expert beats say the spark ignited the helium.
Correction: All sixteen gas cells held hydrogen — the US helium embargo meant she never carried helium. Shot and script line must both say hydrogen.
Source: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

Problem: Brief puts the airship 300–400 ft up with ground crews already hauling on the ropes.
Correction: Sources put her at 180–295 ft when forward lines dropped at 7:21 PM and near 200 ft at 7:25 PM — 300–400 ft is at or above the highest figure.
Source: Airships.net; Commerce Dept board of inquiry, 1937

Problem: Same brief has the zeppelin burst into flames directly above the captain.
Correction: First flames appeared at the stern near gas cells 4 and 5, roughly 500 ft aft of the control car; the control-car crew felt a shudder rather than seeing fire overhead.

Problem: Brief shows the ship's port windows blowing out with orange smoke, in CU on several portholes.
Correction: At about 9:00 AM the steel hatch cover over Hold 4 was blown off and a column of yellow-orange nitrogen-dioxide smoke rose from the open hold — the portholes were not the vent.

Problem: Brief names the ship 'SS Grand Camp' as two words.
Correction: She was the SS Grandcamp, one word — a French-flag Liberty ship, so hull lettering reads GRANDCAMP under the French ensign.

Problem: Briefs stage a casual kids' pickup baseball game at the moment of the blast.
Correction: The Grandcamp blew up at 9:12 AM on Wednesday 16 April 1947, a school-day morning — confirm the witness account before generating children at leisure.

Problem: Briefs show a bucket brigade passing water down a line of workers in the hold.
Correction: Accounts describe a single gallon jug and two fire extinguishers before the captain stopped water being used on the cargo — a bucket brigade is not in the record.

Problem: The 27 March eruption shot is briefed with 'less snow than in ref pic'.
Correction: On 27 March 1980 the cone carried its full winter snowpack — more snow than the mid-May reference — blackened by ash around a new 250-ft crater.

Problem: Brief frames the 27 March eruption as a POV from the research station.
Correction: Coldwater II was not occupied until roughly 1 May 1980, so a March view from that post is anachronistic.

Problem: Briefs repeatedly describe Johnston's 'camp' on the ridge.
Correction: Coldwater II was a USGS observation post — a trailer and a vehicle — not a tent camp.
Source: USGS, Legacy of David A. Johnston

Problem: The bulge sequence builds slowly through spreading cracks and ends on ground opening to reveal an orange glow deep down.
Correction: The north flank failed within seconds of the 08:32 M5.1 quake as three grey debris-avalanche blocks; the exposed cryptodome was solidifying dacite — no incandescent orange magma.

Problem: Briefs show Johnston shielding himself, falling, then crawling away before succumbing.
Correction: The lateral blast crossed 6 miles in about a minute at hundreds of mph and swept the post away instantly — a protracted struggle is speculative.

Problem: Four briefs specify a 1930s 'western Chinese' village.
Correction: The 1931 flood was a central and eastern China disaster — Hubei, Hunan, Jiangxi, Anhui, Jiangsu along the middle and lower Yangzi. Architecture, landscape and dress should be middle-Yangzi central China.
Source: Courtney, The Nature of Disaster in China, 2018

Problem: Both snowmelt briefs are slugged 'Winter, mountains' while the beat is explicitly the arrival of spring.
Correction: Slug as spring thaw — softening snowpack, bare rock, swelling meltwater — to match MeltingSnow01 and the beat.

Problem: Neither Wuhan flood brief specifies a time of day, so the artist may render the wall of water in full daylight.
Correction: The dike failed just before 6:00 AM on 27 July 1931 — first-light shots.

Problem: The sequence is built on tens of thousands drowning instantly when the water reached Wuhan.
Correction: Scholarship stresses relatively few Wuhan residents drowned in the initial inundation; most of the ~2 million deaths came from disease and starvation over following months.

Problem: Brief calls for 'a few full lifeboats visible nearby' as Titanic makes its final plunge.
Correction: Titanic's boats left well under capacity (No. 1 carried 12 of 40) and had pulled well clear — any boats in frame should be partly empty and distant.

Problem: SINKS1 shows the stern at 40° with ship lights still on, while SINKS2 shows the detached stern with no lights.
Correction: Survivor testimony has the lights burning until the break-up at roughly 60° — an already-separated stern should be dark, and the lit shot should show the ship still intact.
Source: US Senate and British Inquiry testimony, 1912

Problem: Brief specifies 10 pipe weights in a harness, 8 on the underside and 1 each side.
Correction: NTSB describes 4–6 cylindrical weights per side at roughly 25–30 lb each — reconcile count, placement and the 37 lb in the VO.

Problem: Both taxi shots specify 'Gran Canaria hills visible in background' behind Los Rodeos.
Correction: Los Rodeos is on Tenerife with the island's own La Laguna plateau and Anaga massif behind it; Gran Canaria is 90 km east across open ocean and not visible.

Problem: The beat states the Gran Canaria terminal bomb injured four people.
Correction: The 13:15 explosion in the terminal florist's shop injured eight.

Problem: Brief calls for an ECU of the KLM's wheels leaving the ground milliseconds before impact.
Correction: KLM 4805 had rotated with nose gear up but main gear still on or barely off the runway — main gear, lower fuselage and engines struck Pan Am.

Problem: Both establishers place the tank on the Charles River, framed from the river's opposite shore.
Correction: The tank stood at 529 Commercial Street on Boston's inner harbour opposite Copp's Hill — the far shore is Charlestown and the Navy Yard.

Problem: Brief puts an elevated railway car floating in the molasses wave.
Correction: A tank plate knocked out an upright of the Atlantic Avenue El and the track sagged; the approaching train stopped short and no El car was carried.

Problem: Every BMF brief mandates a heavy fog look, with instructions to 'add more fog' on the day of the collapse.
Correction: 15 January 1919 was an unseasonably mild ~40 °F day with bare streets, and aftermath photographs show bright clear conditions — confirm the fog is deliberate stylisation.

Problem: Briefs are keyed to a VO placing the rupture at 'around 1PM' with a capacity of 2.5 million gallons.
Correction: The tank failed at about 12:30 pm and held roughly 2.3 million gallons. The 50 ft × 90 ft dimensions are correct.

Problem: Brief flies to the summit and tilts down to reveal a lava-filled crater on pre-eruption Krakatoa.
Correction: Krakatoa had been dormant since 1680 — a forested island with quiescent ash-and-pumice craters. It never held an open lava lake.

Problem: The 10 am climactic blast is slugged 'Clear sky. Calm sea.'
Correction: By 10:02 am on 27 August the strait was already ash-darkened from three earlier explosions, with pumice fall and tsunami-disturbed seas.

Problem: Two briefs show a visible shockwave crossing the water and flattening every tree on an island.
Correction: Vegetation was destroyed by pyroclastic surges, ashfall and tsunami; the pressure wave broke windows 160 km away but is not recorded as levelling forests.

Problem: Briefs describe Krakatoa as a single mountain rising from the island.
Correction: Pre-1883 Krakatoa carried three cones — Perboewatan, Danan and the 813 m Rakata.

Shotcodes: CTD_AI_PAO_PiperAlphaExplodes; CTD_AI_PAO_SinkingIntoWater; CTD_AI_PAO_FinalCollapse; CTD_AI_PAO_DavidLooksAtWater; CTD_AI_PAO_DavidJumps; CTD_AI_PAO_BollandsLooksAtRig
Problem: Everything after the first explosion is slugged 'Night', implying a fully dark sky.
Correction: Piper Alpha lay at 58°28′N, where on 6–7 July the sun never falls more than ~9° below the horizon — the 22:20 riser rupture and the 00:45 collapse played out in nautical twilight with a lit northern horizon.

Problem: The same helideck moment is slugged 'Sky at twilight' in two briefs and 'Night' in two others.
Correction: Pick one lighting state for the Kinrade helideck sequence so the cut holds together.

Problem: The sprinkler shot is built on a VO saying the blast disabled the fire sprinkler controls.
Correction: Cullen found the deluge pumps were on manual for diver safety and were never started — the system did not fail because of the explosion.

Problem: Three briefs stage the mayday on a black rotary desk telephone.
Correction: The distress call went out by radio to nearby vessels — confirm the instrument and the 1988-era handset.

Problem: Four briefs show San Francisco row houses cracking and toppling sideways into the street and onto a parked car.
Correction: Marina District failures were soft-storey collapses — upper floors dropping straight down onto crushed ground-floor garages, buildings settling and leaning from liquefaction, not falling across the roadway.

Problem: Street and building shots are slugged 'DAY. SUNNY' with no time-of-day guidance.
Correction: The quake hit at 5:04 pm PDT, about 80 minutes before sunset — low golden light with long shadows.

Problem: Briefs describe Tim Peterson as an Oakland rookie firefighter driving to his station when the viaduct fell.
Correction: Reporting names him Tim Petersen and says he joined Oakland FD after the collapse — his father was the firefighter on scene. Confirm spelling and status.

Problem: The same Industrial Canal sequence is slugged 'Gale force wind' in the levee briefs and 'hurricane force winds' in the canal briefs.
Correction: Settle on one wind state; New Orleans was in hurricane-force winds when the floodwalls went, so the stronger direction is the accurate one.

Problem: Two shots of the same breach wave specify different heights — 20 ft in one, 15 ft in the other.
Correction: Fix a single wave height for the Lower Ninth Ward breach.

Problem: All breach and house-destruction shots are slugged 'EXT. DAY'.
Correction: The first Industrial Canal breach came around 5 am, before a ~6:30 am sunrise; only the larger second breach near 7:45 am was in daylight — confirm which breach this is.

Problem: Briefs specify a '4,000 pound engine' sliding down the runway; a beat elsewhere calls engine-plus-pylon 9,000 lb.
Correction: The separated CF6 engine and pylon assembly weighed about 13,477 lb — the object must read as a ~6.7-ton assembly.

Problem: Slats04 shows left FLAPS on the BACK of the wing failing to move; Slats02 asks for SLATS on the BACK of the right wing.
Correction: Takeoff flaps stayed extended and symmetric; the failure was the left OUTBOARD LEADING-EDGE SLATS — front of the wing — retracting uncommanded after hydraulic lines were severed.

Problem: Four briefs slug the runway 'DAY — SUMMER, HAZY' with heat shimmer.
Correction: 15:04 on 25 May 1979: sky clear, visibility 15 miles, 63 °F, wind 020 at 22 kt gusting 28 — a bright sharp late-spring afternoon with no heat haze.

Problem: Brief calls for a CU of the pilot's HAND adjusting the rudder.
Correction: The DC-10 rudder is commanded by foot pedals — the shot is feet on the pedals, hands staying on the control wheel.

Problem: The wide DC-10 cockpit brief populates the flight deck with two crew only.
Correction: Flight 191 carried three — Captain Lux, First Officer Dillard and Flight Engineer Udovich at the right-hand side panel, which must be occupied in a wide shot.

Problem: Briefs place photographer Michael Laughlin in an O'Hare parking lot in airline-pilot dress.
Correction: Contemporaneous captions describe him as a 24-year-old student pilot on a layover in the terminal — confirm both vantage and wardrobe.

Shotcodes: CTD_AI_CCS_LifeboatEvacuation01; CTD_AI_CCS_LifeboatEvacuation02; CTD_AI_CCS_LifeboatEvacuation03; CTD_AI_CCS_LifeboatEvacuation04; CTD_AI_CCS_LifeboatEvacuation05; CTD_AI_CCS_LifeboatEvacuation06
Problem: All six lifeboat briefs lock the ship 'listing at 50%', including passengers stepping from the hull into a boat.
Correction: Abandon ship came at 22:54:10 and the first boats went down at 22:55 with the list at roughly 11–20° (25–30° only by 23:11). Launching at 50° is impossible — these need a shallow list.
Source: Italian MIT Marine Casualties Investigative Body, 2013

Problem: Restaurant briefs dress the Davises for a 'warm weather cruise' and passengers line an open deck in the same register.
Correction: 21:45 on 13 January 2012 off Giglio, NE force-4 sea and 17-knot wind — wardrobe should read mid-winter Mediterranean.

Problem: Brief fixes the ship at 50° to starboard at the moment it 'has now settled on rock'.
Correction: The list passed 25–30° at 23:11 and rose sharply after midnight to about 80° — 50° corresponds to a narrow window around 00:00, not the settled state.

Problem: The shot slugged for the captain's 'Hard to starboard!' order actually describes Schettino holding his date's hand, duplicating JUL9HoldHands word for word.
Correction: Re-brief to the helm order so it pairs with HardToStarboard02's wheel CU.

Problem: Ship-to-shore distance is specified four different ways across one continuous sail-past: 250 m, 300 m, 1 km and 'about a mile'.
Correction: Fix a single distance ladder — the ship closed from roughly 0.5 nm to under 300 m before contact — so shore-light scale is consistent.

Problem: Both briefs render the spilled benzol as a 'tar-like substance' pouring thickly across the deck.
Correction: Benzol was a high-octane motor fuel of benzene and toluene — a thin, clear, fast-evaporating liquid that spreads and flashes off, nothing like tar.
Source: Maritime Museum of the Atlantic; Halifax Explosion historiography

Problem: Briefs light the fire with sparks from the ship's engines, with a CU of the engine throwing sparks into spilled fuel.
Correction: Ignition came from steel-on-steel sparks as Imo's bow ground out of Mont-Blanc's hull; vapour caught at the waterline and ran up the hull. Shoot the gash, not the engine room.

Problem: Brief stages Mackey's survival as a POV from his lifeboat as the blast hurls the boat into a tree.
Correction: Mackey had already landed on the Dartmouth shore and was on foot with Captain Le Medec when the blast knocked them down — a shoreline run, not a boat in flight.
Source: Library and Archives Canada, Mackey's own account

Problem: Brief calls for large crates stencilled 'DANGER: TNT' burning on Mont-Blanc's deck.
Correction: The TNT, picric acid and guncotton were stowed below in the holds and the ship carried no hazard markings; only benzol drums were on deck.

Problem: The beat sizes the harbour tsunami at 'a giant wave, 20 feet high'.
Correction: The displacement wave ran up to about 18 m (roughly 60 ft) above high-water on the Dartmouth side — confirm the intended figure before scaling.

Problem: Beats state Imo's departure had been delayed three days and that she was setting off 'for Belgium'.
Correction: She was held that same evening because her coal arrived late and the nets had closed, and she was bound for New York to load Belgian relief supplies.

Shotcodes: CTD_AI_LMR_TrainStatic01; CTD_AI_LMR_BehindLastCar; CTD_AI_LMR_TrainHeadOn; CTD_AI_LMR_TrainIncline; CTD_AI_LMR_StopWithSmoke; CTD_AI_LMR_Outskirts01; CTD_AI_LMR_FlyIntoEngine01
Problem: Every train brief shows a single locomotive hauling the 72 tank cars.
Correction: MMA-002 ran with a five-locomotive head-end consist (MMA 5017 leading) plus a VB buffer car and a box car ahead of the tank cars.

Problem: Hand-brake briefs put Harding crouching at a hand brake on a tank car that looms over him.
Correction: The seven hand brakes were applied on the five locomotives and the buffer car at the head end — none on any tank car.

Problem: Both briefs show flames already erupting from the locomotive as Harding's taxi pulls onto the highway.
Correction: The taxi collected Harding at about 23:30 when the driver saw heavy smoke and oil droplets; fire was only reported at 23:50 — confirm this is intended dramatisation.

Problem: Brief shows a gloved hand throwing a protruding lever on the in-cab console to shut the locomotive down.
Correction: TSB records the lead locomotive shut down with the emergency fuel cut-off switch — confirm the exact control and its location.

Problem: The beat states 'two million gallons of crude oil starts gushing out'.
Correction: The train carried about 7.7 million litres and roughly 6 million litres (about 1.6 million US gallons) were released — scale the slick accordingly.

Problem: VO says the train is hauling 72 tankers loaded with 'ten thousand tons of crude oil'.
Correction: About 10,290 tons was the weight of the whole train; the crude itself was 7.7 million litres, roughly 6,400 tonnes.

Problem: Both wind briefs are driven by 'On the morning of October 8th, a cold front sweeps in' and lit as ground-level daylight.
Correction: The wind shift and fire run happened on the EVENING of Sunday 8 October 1871 — dusk/dark, wind from the southwest ahead of the low.
Source: NOAA NWS Green Bay, The Peshtigo Fire

Shotcodes: CTD_AI_PFS_WallOfFlames01; CTD_AI_PFS_WallOfFlames02; CTD_AI_PFS_TornadoFireball01; CTD_AI_PFS_TornadoFireball02; CTD_AI_PFS_TornadoFireball03; CTD_AI_PFS_PeshtigoBurns; CTD_AI_PFS_SandToGlass
Problem: None of the firestorm briefs carry a time-of-day slug, so they will default to daylight renders.
Correction: The firestorm reached Peshtigo after dark on 8 October 1871 — every one of these must be slugged NIGHT, lit only by fire.

Problem: Brief calls for a CU of riverside sand visibly melting into glass on the strength of a '2,000 degrees' beat.
Correction: The 2,000 °F figure comes from fire-service literature while silica needs roughly 3,000 °F to fuse — the sand-to-glass image is a disputed legend.
Source: Wildland Fire Foundation Peshtigo staff-ride document, 2025

Problem: Beat gives frontal winds 'of up to 100 miles an hour'.
Correction: There were no instrument observations; NWS reconstruction gives strong southwesterly gradient winds, and 100–110 mph describes fire-generated whirlwinds rather than the front.

Problem: Both drought briefs are pitched as 'late summer vibe' baking under intense sun, though the VO runs to October 1871.
Correction: Fix the intended month — early-October Wisconsin (70s, autumn foliage, low sun) reads differently from mid-summer, and both briefs must match.

Problem: Both rescue briefs are driven by 'It takes two hours to dig their way to Choi Myong Suk', staging a short entombment.
Correction: Choi Myung-seok, 21, was pulled from a 1.2 × 1.5 m void near a basement escalator at 08:20 on 9 July 1995 — eleven days and about 230 hours after the collapse.

Problem: The three collapse briefs describe the whole store pancaking to the ground.
Correction: Only the SOUTH wing collapsed (all but its southernmost section) in under 20 seconds; the north wing stayed standing — exteriors must keep an intact structure beside the rubble.

Problem: Brief shows a top-down atrium shot of a crowd streaming out of every floor on the 17:50 evacuation beat.
Correction: Management kept the store trading all day and only the fifth floor was closed; roughly 1,500 people were still inside at 17:52 — a store-wide orderly exodus overstates the record.

Problem: Two briefs covering the same basement moment contradict each other: one asks for people out of focus in the background, the other specifies 'No other people'.
Correction: Pick one treatment for the basement food-court beat so the two shots cut together.

Problem: The disaster sequence is slugged DAWN, EARLY MORNING, DAY and 'hot, hazy summer day', with the resident stepping into 'full morning light'.
Correction: The pipe failed about 05:35 and the cloud ignited about 05:45 on 19 November 1984, before nautical twilight (05:57, sunrise 06:46) — the whole sequence plays in full darkness lit only by the flare pit and fires.
Source: HSE COMAH case study, PEMEX LPG Terminal, 1984

Problem: Aerial brief follows the vapour cloud drifting across the facility at about 40 ft up.
Correction: The cloud was a ground-hugging layer roughly 200 × 150 m and only 2 m (about 7 ft) deep as it rolled toward the flare pit — which is why it found the ignition source.

Problem: Beat limits hot metal fragments to 'as far as 600 feet away'.
Correction: BLEVE fragments, some up to 30 tonnes, were thrown to 350 m in public areas with the furthest at 1,200 m — the debris field is far larger.

Problem: Cloud briefs contradict each other: one wants rapidly escaping white vapour, another says make it barely visible, a third abandons the cloud for a POV creep.
Correction: Settle one treatment — dense white condensation mist at the rupture thinning to near-invisible as it drifts — so the three read as one cloud.

Problem: Both briefs direct the fire ladders to extend and stop at the 7th floor.
Correction: The FDNY's longest 1911 ladder reached only the 6th floor — three storeys below the trapped workers on the 9th.
Source: Cornell ILR Kheel Center; FDNY demonstration

Problem: Shepherd is shown typing his famous account on a typewriter in a house den.
Correction: Shepherd phoned his account in live from the scene while the fire burned; Roy Howard took the dictation and telegraphed it out.

Problem: A lit cigarette sits in an ashtray beside a woman's sewing machine, with a rack focus onto it.
Correction: Smoking was banned inside Triangle and done concealed by male cutters; the Fire Marshal attributed ignition to a hidden match or cigarette dropped into a scrap bin under a cutting table.

Problem: Both records are filed under TSF but their creative direction is 'INT. RESTAURANT, NIGHT' and points artists at CCS_Stampede01/02.
Correction: These are another story's briefs mis-filed into the Triangle sequence — remove or re-slug before they go out as Asch Building shots.

Problem: A fire inspector telephones Blanck and Harris in June 1909 to arrange a safety meeting, and Blanck hangs up.
Correction: The documented pre-fire approaches were written, unanswered correspondence about fire drills, not a telephone call.
Source: Cornell ILR Kheel Center; trial record

Shotcodes: CTD_AI_TSF_FireEscapeCollapse A; CTD_AI_TSF_FireEscapeCollapse C; CTD_AI_TSF_FireEscapeCollapse D
Problem: The fire escape is framed against 'EXT. ASCH BUILDING' with a birds-eye fall straight to the street.
Correction: The single fire escape was in the enclosed rear courtyard and terminated over a second-floor skylight, not on the public street facade.

Shotcodes: CTD_AI_ORA_PortholeSmashed; CTD_AI_ORA_ControlPanelDamaged A; CTD_AI_ORA_ControlPanelDamaged B; CTD_AI_ORA_ControlPanelDamaged C; CTD_AI_ORA_CrewAtControlPanel A; CTD_AI_ORA_CrewAtControlPanel B; CTD_AI_ORA_CrewAtControlPanel C
Problem: The whole broken-porthole and damaged-ballast-panel sequence is slugged INT. BALLAST CONTROL ROOM — DAY.
Correction: The portlight broke and water reached the panel between roughly 19:00 and 21:00 on 14 February, hours after a ~17:20 winter sunset — it must be night, as sibling briefs already specify.
Source: Royal Commission on the Ocean Ranger Marine Disaster, 1984

Problem: Men in the water without survival suits is slugged EXT. NORTH ATLANTIC — DAY while every other brief in the sequence is NIGHT.
Correction: The crew abandoned the rig from about 01:30 and were in the sea until it sank around 03:10 on 15 February — full darkness.

Problem: Briefs are built to sell the expert line that the rig is 'the length of two football fields'.
Correction: Ocean Ranger was 396 ft long and 262 ft wide — barely more than one football field. The '35 storeys high' figure is correct.

Problem: The liferaft canister is specified as 2.5 m long and 0.1 m high.
Correction: 0.1 m is physically impossible — a small offshore canister is roughly 0.5–0.6 m in diameter and moulded GRP, not white metal.

Problem: The lifeboat-inventory shots are specified as a 'sunny, warm winter day' with calm seas on the Grand Banks in February 1982.
Correction: 'Warm' will push the generator to summer light — specify cold, low, hard winter light over a calm sea to match the other February exteriors.

Problem: Three ECUs of the altimeter read 30,400 ft at the moment the captain requests a higher level.
Correction: KE007 was cruising at FL330 when it requested FL350, and was at 35,000 ft when the missile hit — 30,400 ft matches neither.

Problem: The slugline reads 'EXT. KAL007 (727)', which will cue a Boeing 727 nose.
Correction: KAL 007 was a Boeing 747-230B (HL7442) — the wide-body nose specified everywhere else in the story.

Problem: The aircraft is directed to nose-dive from cruise straight into the sea.
Correction: After the detonation KE007 arced upward for about 113 seconds, descended gradually, levelled at 16,424 ft for roughly five minutes, then spiralled down — about 12 minutes of flight.

Problem: The impact shot specifies 'rough waters' while the debris shot moments later specifies a 'calm ocean surface'.
Correction: Pick one sea state for the Moneron Island impact and carry it across both shots.

Problem: The deck crew is shown shovelling and levelling black asphalt with an asphalt roller in the foreground.
Correction: The 1 August 2007 job was concrete resurfacing — milling 2 in of concrete wearing course and placing a new 2 in concrete overlay, with aggregate piles, cement and water tankers and a concrete mixer on the deck.

Problem: Jeff Ringate is placed on the riverbank, fishing Lindsay Walz out from the shore.
Correction: Ringate was a construction worker who fell with the bridge; he spotted Walz from the collapsed deck and pulled her up onto it with a broom handle.

Problem: The beat states hundreds of vehicles plunge 110 ft into the Mississippi.
Correction: 111 vehicles were on the collapsed portion and only 17 were recovered from the water; the main span fell 108 ft into a river 15 ft deep.

Problem: A mid-1990s inspector hammer-taps visibly corroding gusset plates, framed as the discovery that mattered.
Correction: NTSB found the cause was under-thickness U10 gusset plates — a 1960s design error, not corrosion; corrosion at L11 was expressly excluded as causal.

Problem: Ringate is locked in as a recurring on-screen character described as a 'tall, blonde, Caucasian 20-year-old'.
Correction: No published account gives his age or appearance — confirm before building a recognisable likeness of a named living person across multiple shots.

Problem: Ignition is staged as an exposed cable wire on the mine floor throwing a spark into built-up methane.
Correction: MSHA determined lightning was the most likely ignition source and that the explosion occurred inside the sealed 2 North Mains area, where no cables or working faces existed.
Source: MSHA Report of Investigation, Sago Mine, 2007

Problem: Supervisors stand outside in overcast winter DAY at the 6:26 am explosion, and the escaping crew exits into DAY at about 7:30 am.
Correction: Sunrise at Sago on 2 January 2006 was about 7:40 am EST — the explosion happened in full darkness and the crew surfaced in dim pre-sunrise twilight.
Source: MSHA, 2007; NOAA solar position, Upshur County WV

Problem: Miners gear up with 'oxygen masks' around their necks, and underground one is taken off and put back on.
Correction: Sago miners carried belt-worn CSE SR-100 self-rescuers — single-use chemical-oxygen canisters that cannot be doffed and re-donned once started.

Problem: A miner drills the coal face with a hand-held jackhammer and roof bolts are driven with a sledgehammer.
Correction: Each Sago section worked with two remote-controlled continuous mining machines and two twin-boom roof-bolting machines — no hand drilling or hammered bolts.

Problem: Multiple briefs specify a mine ceiling around 6 ft with miners moving crouched.
Correction: Average mining height at Sago was approximately 7 ft — the men could walk upright.

Problem: Two versions of the same establishing sequence are dated 'Grey, Autumn Day 2005' and 'Grey, Autumn Day 2006'.
Correction: Fix one date — the disaster is early January, so autumn 2006 post-dates the event it is establishing.

Problem: Both briefs direct red-hot lava flowing down the side of the mountain.
Correction: No lava was produced in AD 79 — it was a Plinian pumice fall followed by pyroclastic density currents, so the mountainside carries ash and glowing surges, never lava streams.
Source: Sigurdsson et al., The Eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79

Problem: Pre-eruption Pompeii shots call for 'dormant Mt. Vesuvius' in the background, which will generate today's familiar cone.
Correction: The modern Gran Cono post-dates AD 79; in 62–79 AD Vesuvius was a single, taller, vine-covered summit inside a pre-existing caldera rim, and its top was destroyed in the eruption.

Problem: The pyroclastic surge that kills the Pompeians is slugged EXT. POMPEII — NIGHT.
Correction: The surge arrived about 07:30 on the morning of the second day — the blackness is ash-cloud darkness, so light it as daylight extinguished rather than a night scene.

Problem: The shot populates Pompeii's streets with Roman soldiers alongside villagers.
Correction: Pompeii was a civilian colonia with no standing garrison — confirm before dressing legionaries into an everyday street scene.

Problem: The 'just after flooding moment' version, in which a house is torn from its foundations, is slugged DAY in overcast daylight.
Correction: In Altenahr the house that broke loose went at about 21:50 on 14 July, after a ~21:30 sunset, and the flood peaked around 23:00 in full darkness.

Problem: The Sermanns' escape upstairs is slugged DUSK, yet the following brief shows the sun setting only after they are already up there.
Correction: Lukas Sermann and his father were cut off at about 19:00 on 14 July — broad overcast daylight in mid-July Germany — so the escape is a daylight scene and the dusk time-lapse follows it.

Problem: Lukas and his father shoulder open a door and scramble up flooded wooden stairs onto a balcony.
Correction: The published reconstruction has them stranded in the current and breaking into an ice cream shop for shelter — confirm the balcony detail.

Problem: The beat states seven people drowned at the campsite in Dorsel.
Correction: Regional records for Campingplatz Stahlhütte give six deaths; the site flooded around 16:00 on 14 July, which does support the DAY slug.

Problem: The same stretch of the Ahr is specified as 9 m wide in one brief and 12 m wide in the others.
Correction: Fix a single channel width so the pre-flood and flood-moment shots cut together.

Problem: The Altenahr riverbank explainer is specified as a sunny, cloudless day with sun sparkling on the water.
Correction: Every other Ahr brief is locked to overcast grey with rain or mist — a cloudless plate will not cut into the sequence.

Problem: The 1 May detection flight is specified as 'sun shining through overcast skies', with a yellow helicopter carrying a 245-gallon belly tank.
Correction: 1 May 2016 sat under an omega-block ridge with record heat, single-digit humidity and strong winds — hot hazy sun, not overcast — and the documented initial-attack machines were Bell 407/212s making slung-bucket drops.

Problem: All five briefs show subway station lights physically cutting out at the '7pm' beat, treating the shutdown as a blackout.
Correction: The 7 pm Sunday 28 October event was Cuomo's suspension of subway, bus and rail service — stations stayed lit; darkness came the following night with the Con Edison outage and station flooding.
Source: MTA service suspension order, 28 Oct 2012; NHC report AL182012

Problem: The briefs commit to specific visuals for the Tommy Woods anecdote — Belle Harbor, 4-ft floodwater, burning houses — but the anecdote could not be corroborated.
Correction: Confirm the source interview, location and water depth; Belle Harbor fires are documented (32 buildings lost on Newport Avenue), so the burning background is safe but the depth and street are not.
Source: IAFSS, Fires During the 2012 Hurricane Sandy in Queens, 2013

Problem: Both briefs read only 'POV of driver on rural road in Africa at night', which will generate a generic African savanna road.
Correction: The 15 August 1984 event is the Lake Monoun gas burst in Cameroon's West Region — the road runs through hilly, densely cultivated volcanic highlands near Njindoun, not savanna.
Source: Sigurdsson et al., J. Volcanology and Geothermal Research, 1987

Problem: The beat places the truck driving into the whitish cloud 'around 10:30 at night'.
Correction: The report from the lake was heard about 22:30, but the deaths on the road — including the lorry carrying twelve people whose engine stalled — occurred between 03:00 and dawn.

Problem: The Black Friday blackout shots specify settled post-storm conditions — snow, ice-coated trees, no falling precipitation — at the moment the Montreal grid fails.
Correction: The 9 January 1998 collapse happened during the third and final wave of freezing rain (78 mm over roughly 80 hours ending 10 January), so freezing rain or drizzle should probably still be falling.
Source: Hydro-Québec ice storm chronology; Environment Canada

Problem: The beat says the landslide pushed 'more than 270 million tons of water up and over the dam'.
Correction: 270 million cubic metres is the volume of ROCK that fell into the reservoir; only about 25–50 million m³ of water overtopped the dam.
Source: Italian Dept of Civil Protection; ASDSO Dam Failures case study

Problem: Every 9 October night brief is slugged 'Overcast. DARK.' with no precipitation.

Problem: The beat states that 'by late September' engineers were seeing the mountain slip about eight inches a day.
Correction: Movement was around 2 cm per day on 25 September 1963 and only reached about 20 cm a day in the first days of October, immediately before the collapse.
